1. Establishing a Connection: What a Remote Really Is

A remote typically uses a bare repository without a working tree, but it can also point to another local or server-side repository. Above all, a “remote” is a configured address and refspec. Before synchronizing, establish the "contract" between your local repository and the remote.

2. Three Ways to Authenticate with GitHub: Setup and Platform Differences
A. HTTPS: Simple, but Requires Credential Management
Address format: https://example.com/team/project.git
Mechanism: use a PAT, OAuth credentials managed by a credential helper, or other supported credentials. Never put tokens in a remote URL or public configuration.
Platform-Specific Setup
Windows: Git for Windows includes Git Credential Manager, which handles OAuth pop-up windows automatically.
Arch Linux: use an actual Git credential helper and configure its secure storage backend. git-delta displays diffs; it does not store credentials.
NixOS: programs.git.enable = true; enables Git, but does not automatically set up HTTPS credential storage. Configure a credential helper separately.
B. SSH: Asymmetric Encryption for Professional Development (Recommended)
Address format: git@example.com:team/project.git

Mechanism: authenticate with an Ed25519 or RSA public/private key pair. You can protect the private key with a passphrase and use an agent; avoiding an account-password prompt does not mean the private key has no passphrase.
Platform-Specific Setup and Key Generation

Windows: run the command above in Git Bash. Keys are stored in %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\.
Arch Linux: install openssh. sudo pacman -S openssh
NixOS: the SSH client connects to Git servers. Outbound Git access does not require enabling services.openssh.enable, which starts the local SSH server. Configure the client and agent as needed.

5. Collaborative Workflows: The PR / MR Model
Fork: clone someone else's repository into your own account through the web interface.
Clone: use git clone to get a local copy.
Develop: create a new branch for development.
Push: push to your own remote.
Pull Request (PR): use the web interface to ask the original author to merge your changes.

With a typical fetch configuration, this updates origin/* and fork/* and prunes stale tracking references for branches deleted remotely. It does not overwrite your local development branches with remote content. origin/main:main means "use the local tracking reference for the original repository as the source to update the fork's main." This step does not require your local main to be synchronized, and it does not update other development branches in the fork. These three development branches correspond to only two open PRs. A merged branch may remain in the fork, and fork/HEAD should not be counted as a fourth development branch. Before cleaning up, check current PR status, the merge method, and whether unique commits remain. Do not delete branches based on their count alone.
6. Common Pain Points and Best Practices: Resolving Conflicts Gracefully
Scenario: A Push Fails Because Multiple People Modified the Same Remote Branch
The following approach is suitable for local commits that have not yet been shared. For shared history, use merge or another coordinated approach according to team policy:
git commit (save local changes).
git fetch origin (retrieve the latest remote snapshot).
git rebase origin/master (replay local commits on top of the remote history).
Review the rebase result and run tests, then git push. Further remote updates or protection rules may still cause rejection.
A Closer Look: Why Can git push -f Be Disastrous?
When you run git push -f, you are effectively telling the server: "Ignore what everyone else committed and forcibly replace the remote branch with my current state."
Example scenario:
Shared starting point: you and colleague A both have Commit 1 -> Commit 2.
Colleague A commits: they develop a feature and push, so the remote is now 1 -> 2 -> 3.
You rewrite history: you decide the local Commit 2 could be better and modify it with rebase or amend. Your local history becomes 1 -> 2'(新哈希).
You run Push -f: you forcibly change the server's history to 1 -> 2'. Colleague A's Commit 3 disappears from the remote!
Disaster Strikes
: when colleague A synchronizes again, their local and remote histories may diverge, requiring reconciliation with the rewritten history. Git finds that:
The local Commit 3 is based on the old Commit 2.
But the remote now has 2'.

This can lead to extremely complex conflicts. If they handle them incorrectly, for example by merging directly, they may bring back old code you had removed and even turn the project's entire history topology into a tangled mess.
Coordinate any rewriting of shared-branch history in advance, and check the server's protection rules. Do not conceal an ordinary synchronization failure with a force push.
A Safer Approach: --force-with-lease

If you must force-push, for example on your own isolated feature branch, use: git push --force-with-lease Mechanism: it requires the remote reference to match an expected value. Without an explicit expected value, it usually relies on the local remote-tracking reference. Background fetches may refresh that reference and weaken the protection. When strict constraints are needed, first record and verify the tip you are allowed to replace, then explicitly specify the remote branch and expected commit:
A lease cannot determine whether overwritten commits are valuable, nor can it automatically recover accidentally deleted data.
7. Permission Management: Who Can Push Code?

Distributed history does not itself grant write access to remotes. Servers can control reads and pushes through SSH/HTTP authentication, filesystem permissions, receive hooks, and hosting-platform rules. Permission control is not exclusive to hosting platforms.
A. Repository Access Levels (Using GitHub as an Example)
Public: anyone can read (Clone/Fetch), but only "collaborators" can write (Push).
Private: access can be granted through individuals, organization teams, apps, deployment credentials, and other mechanisms, with read and write permissions controlled separately.
Collaboration Roles
Read: can read and participate in relevant discussions, but generally cannot push code.
Write: can push code directly to unprotected branches.
Maintain/Admin: maintainer and administrator permissions differ. Sensitive settings, such as deleting a repository, typically require administrator privileges; verify the platform's role definitions.
B. Branch Protection Rules (Protected Branches)
On a professional team, having "write access" does not mean you can do anything you please.
Restrict direct pushes: teams typically lock down main or master, preventing anyone from using push directly.
Require Pull Requests: all code must be developed on a branch -> submitted as a PR -> merged by someone with the appropriate merge permissions after the required reviews and automated checks pass.
Restrict force pushes: push -f is disabled on protected branches by default.

A Philosophical Note
The highest purpose of permission management is to prevent mistakes, not merely to deter bad actors. Good rules let team members experiment freely on feature branches without breaking the mainline code.
